topics.title: Toothbrushing Guide
bullets: Brush twice a day, for about 2 minutes each time.
Place the brush with the bristles tilted slightly towards the gumline and use short, gentle strokes (modified Bass technique, for older children and adults).
Young children: small circular movements (Fones technique) with a parent helping.
Clean the outer, inner and chewing surfaces of every tooth, including along the gumline.
Spit out the toothpaste. Do not rinse with water straight away.
Sources: [MOH Malaysia, Program Ikon Gigi (iGG) module](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/garispanduan/Modul%20Ikon%20Gigi%20-%20SET%201.pdf)
why: Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria that builds up on teeth every day.
Bacteria in plaque make acids that can cause tooth decay and inflamed gums.
Brushing removes plaque. Spitting out (not rinsing) leaves fluoride on your teeth to keep protecting them.

topics.title: Toothbrushes: Choosing and Using
bullets: Choose a soft-bristled brush. Hard bristles can wear away gums and tooth surfaces.
A small brush head reaches the back teeth more easily. The handle should feel comfortable to hold.
Manual and electric brushes can both clean well when used properly. An electric brush may help people who find manual brushing difficult.
Replace your toothbrush about every 3 months, or sooner if the bristles are bent or frayed, and after an illness.
Brush gently. Pressing hard does not clean better and can hurt your gums.
**Manual or electric?** Both clean well when used properly. A powered toothbrush can help people with limited dexterity and children who need encouragement.

**Bristles:** soft, medium and hard bristles are sold. Soft bristles are recommended because they remove plaque well and are gentler on the gums and teeth. Medium and hard bristles may damage the gums and wear away tooth surfaces, especially if you brush hard.
**Head design:** choose a small to medium head that reaches the back teeth. Tapered, angled or V-shaped heads can help in some situations, but good technique matters more than design.
**See also:** [Brushing Techniques](topic:25) · [Adaptive Toothbrushes and Aids (Special Needs/OKU)](topic:31)
Sources: [MOH Malaysia, Program Ikon Gigi (iGG) module](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/garispanduan/Modul%20Ikon%20Gigi%20-%20SET%201.pdf)
why: Soft bristles remove plaque without damaging gums.
Worn bristles clean less well.
Gentle, thorough brushing matters more than pressure.

media.required: Photo: manual and electric toothbrushes, and soft, medium and hard bristles compared
media.what: Shows a manual and a powered toothbrush side by side, with labelled close-ups of soft, medium and hard bristles

topics.title: Choosing the Right Toothpaste
bullets: Fluoride toothpaste helps strengthen teeth and prevent tooth decay.
Do not swallow toothpaste. Spit it out after brushing.
Young children need an adult to supervise brushing.
**Read the label:** look for fluoride and the amount in ppm. Most daily toothpastes contain fluoride.
**Sensitive teeth:** toothpaste made for sensitive teeth can help when used regularly. Ask your dental team if the pain does not settle.
**Whitening toothpaste:** it can remove surface stains but does not change the natural colour of teeth, and some are abrasive or cause sensitivity. Choose one that contains fluoride.
**High-fluoride toothpaste:** a stronger fluoride toothpaste may be prescribed for people at high risk of decay. Use it only on a dentist’s advice.
**Special conditions:** people with dry mouth, gum problems or other conditions may need a particular toothpaste. Ask your dentist.
why: Fluoride makes tooth enamel stronger and helps teeth resist acid attacks from plaque.
Young children often swallow toothpaste. Too much fluoride while permanent teeth are forming can cause white or brown marks (fluorosis), so small children use less.
The right amount balances protection and safety, so brush twice a day with the right amount.
warnings: DRAFT · pending verification against current MOH Malaysia guidance

Amount and fluoride strength: MOH Malaysia’s 2022 toddler guideline advises brushing at least twice a day with a smear or pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for ages 1 to 4 years. The exact amount for each age and the fluoride strength still need confirmation by the dental team.
notes: 🔎 Check the tube: choose a fluoride toothpaste with at least 1000 ppm fluoride.
👪 Parents: put the toothpaste on the brush yourself and supervise brushing.

topics.title: How to Floss
bullets: Brushing cannot reach between teeth. Cleaning there once a day helps protect your gums.
Floss: slide it gently between teeth, curve it in a C shape around each tooth and move it up and down.
Interdental brushes may suit people with wider gaps, braces or gum problems. Ask your dental team for the right size.
With braces, use a floss threader or interdental brush.
why: A toothbrush cannot reach the tight spaces between teeth.
Plaque left there can irritate gums and contribute to decay between teeth.
Cleaning between teeth once a day helps keep gums healthy.

media.required: Flossing demonstration
media.what: Shows the C-shape technique and a floss holder for people with limited dexterity
media.video_title: How to Floss Step by Step

topics.title: Oral Health and Dental Diseases
bullets: These are summaries for general information. Only a dental professional can tell what is causing your symptoms.

**Dental caries (tooth decay):** damage to teeth caused by acids from plaque bacteria and sugars. It may show as white or brown spots, holes or toothache. Prevent it with fluoride toothpaste, fewer sugary snacks and regular check-ups.
**Gingivitis:** inflamed gums caused by plaque. Gums may look red or swollen and bleed when brushing. It can often be reversed with good brushing and cleaning between teeth.

**Periodontitis:** a more serious gum disease that damages the tissues and bone holding teeth. Signs may include gums pulling away, bad breath that does not go away, and loose teeth. It needs professional care.

**Halitosis (bad breath):** often comes from plaque and bacteria on the teeth, gums and tongue. Brush, clean between teeth and gently clean your tongue. Persistent bad breath should be checked by a dental professional.

**Tooth sensitivity:** short, sharp pain with cold, hot, sweet or touch, which can happen when dentine is exposed. Brush gently with a soft brush. See a dentist if it lasts or is severe, as there are several possible causes.
**Seek dental care promptly if** you have toothache, swelling of the face or gums, gums that bleed often, loose teeth, a mouth ulcer that does not heal in about 3 weeks, or pain that does not settle.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)
why: Many dental problems start quietly, without pain.
Early care is simpler, cheaper and gentler than treating advanced problems.
Self-diagnosis can be wrong, because one symptom can have several causes.

media.required: Overview: five common oral conditions
media.what: Labelled illustrations of dental caries, gingivitis, periodontitis, halitosis and tooth sensitivity

topics.title: Children’s Oral Health
bullets: Start brushing as soon as the first tooth appears. Parents should brush young children’s teeth and supervise until the child can brush well.
Use fluoride toothpaste in the amount suited to your child’s age (see the toothpaste module). Help your child spit it out.
Limit sugary drinks and snacks. Offer water and keep sweet foods to mealtimes where possible.
Do not let your child sleep with a bottle of milk or a sweet drink.
Baby teeth matter: they help with chewing and speech and guide adult teeth into place. Decay in baby teeth can cause pain and infection.
Visit the dental clinic regularly for check-ups and preventive care, even when there is no pain.
why: Early cavities can start soon after teeth appear, and they can be prevented.
Children cannot brush well alone because their hand skills are still developing.
Frequent sugar means more acid attacks on teeth.
warnings: Age for independent brushing and recommended visit interval for children: confirm against current MOH Malaysia guidance.

topics.title: Adult Oral Health
bullets: Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between your teeth once a day.
Limit how often you have sugary foods and drinks, especially between meals.
Healthy gums do not usually bleed or hurt. Bleeding when you brush is a sign to clean more carefully, and to see a dental professional if it continues.
Smoking harms the gums and slows healing. Stopping helps your mouth and your whole body; ask your clinic about support.
Have regular dental check-ups so problems are found early.
why: Most gum disease and decay can be prevented with daily habits.
Smoking raises the risk of gum disease and mouth cancer.
Early problems often cause no pain.
warnings: Recommended check-up interval for adults: confirm against current MOH Malaysia guidance.

topics.title: Older Adults’ Oral Health
bullets: Keep brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, even if you have few teeth. Clean your gums and tongue too.
Dry mouth raises the risk of decay, including on exposed root surfaces. Sip water often, and ask your dentist or pharmacist if a medicine is causing it.
Denture wearers: see the Dentures module for daily cleaning and night-time care.
Caregivers: help with brushing and denture cleaning for people who cannot do it themselves, in a gentle and patient way.
Keep visiting the dentist regularly, even if you wear dentures.
why: Gums can recede with age, exposing roots that decay more easily.
Many medicines reduce saliva, which normally protects teeth.
A clean mouth helps comfort and eating.

topics.title: Special Oral Care
bullets: Some people need extra or adapted oral care. Choose a group below to learn more.

topics.title: Special Needs (including OKU)
bullets: Let the person brush as independently as they can, then a caregiver finishes the job.
Sit the person comfortably with the head supported. A thicker or adapted handle, or an electric brush, can help if grip is weak.
Keep a calm daily routine at the same time each day, using simple steps, pictures and praise.
Tell the dental team about medicines, health conditions and what helps the person feel at ease.
**See also:** [Adaptive Toothbrushes and Aids (Special Needs/OKU)](topic:31)
why: Some people find it hard to clean their mouth, or have conditions or medicines that raise the risk of dental problems.
A steady, calm routine makes brushing easier and less stressful over time.
Regular visits help the dental team plan care that suits the person.
warnings: If there is difficulty swallowing or a choking risk, ask the dental team about the safest toothpaste amount and brushing position.

media.required: Assisted toothbrushing for a person with special needs
media.what: Shows a caregiver positioning the person comfortably and brushing step by step

topics.title: Infants & Toddlers
bullets: Before teeth appear, gently wipe the gums with a clean, damp cloth. When the first tooth appears, start brushing it twice a day with a soft, baby-sized brush.
Do not let your baby fall asleep with a bottle of milk or a sweet drink. Move to a cup as advised by your health team.
Do not share spoons or clean a pacifier with your mouth. This can pass germs to your baby.
Bring your baby for a dental visit as soon as teeth appear. Your dental team will advise the best timing.

Sources: [MOH Malaysia, Oral Health Programme: Garis Panduan Perkhidmatan Kesihatan Pergigian Toddler (2022), Appendix 5 Anticipatory Guidance](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/publication/FINAL%20GP%20TODDLER%202022%2010.10.2022.pdf)
why: Baby teeth help with chewing, speaking and saving space for adult teeth.
Decay can start soon after teeth appear.
Milk or sweet drinks around the teeth during sleep keep sugar on them for a long time.
warnings: Fluoride toothpaste amount and timing of the first dental visit for infants: pending clinical review against current MOH Malaysia guidance.

topics.title: Braces & Aligners
bullets: Braces: brush after meals when you can and at least twice a day, cleaning around every bracket, wire and along the gumline.
Use an interdental brush or floss threader to clean around wires and between teeth.
Avoid hard, sticky and sugary foods that can break braces or trap plaque.
Aligners: take them out to eat and drink anything except water. Brush your teeth before putting them back in.
Clean aligners with a soft brush and cool water, wear them as long as your orthodontic team advises, and contact the team if anything breaks.
why: Braces and wires trap plaque, and plaque left around brackets can leave white marks on teeth.
Aligners can hold food and sugary drinks against teeth if worn while eating or drinking.
Healthy gums and clean teeth help treatment go smoothly.

media.required: Interdental brush cleaning around brackets
media.what: Shows an interdental brush cleaning between the wires and brackets

topics.title: Dentures
bullets: Clean dentures every day with a soft brush and mild soap or denture cleaner. Ordinary toothpaste can scratch them.
Clean them over a basin of water or a folded towel so they do not break if dropped.
Brush your gums, tongue and any natural teeth every day with a soft toothbrush.
Take dentures out at night as advised and keep them in water or cleaning solution, away from children and pets.
See your dentist if a denture is loose, cracked or causes sore spots. Do not fix it with glue at home.
why: Plaque and germs build up on dentures just like natural teeth and can cause bad breath and sore, red gums.
Taking dentures out at night lets the gums rest.
Hot water can warp dentures, and damaged dentures can hurt the mouth.
warnings: Overnight denture care and cleaner type: confirm with the treating dentist, as advice can differ for each patient.

media.required: Denture removal and cleaning
media.what: Shows removing partial and complete dentures, cleaning them over a basin of water and storing them

topics.title: Pregnant Women
bullets: Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between your teeth daily. Hormone changes can make gums more likely to swell and bleed.
If morning sickness makes you vomit, rinse your mouth with plain water afterwards and wait a while before brushing, because stomach acid softens the tooth surface.
Eat regular healthy meals and limit sugary snacks.
Dental check-ups and care during pregnancy are important. Tell the dental team that you are pregnant.
why: Hormone changes can make gums react more strongly to plaque.
Stomach acid from vomiting can weaken enamel.
Good oral care now also helps you start healthy habits for your baby.
warnings: Timing of dental treatment and any medicines during pregnancy: the dentist will advise; confirm against current MOH Malaysia guidance.

media.required: Infographic: gum care during pregnancy
media.what: Shows pregnancy-related gum changes and simple daily care steps

topics.title: Dry Mouth
bullets: Dry mouth happens when there is not enough saliva. Common causes include some medicines, certain health conditions and mouth breathing.
Sip water often and have water with meals. Sugar-free gum or lozenges may help the mouth make more saliva.
Avoid sugary drinks and snacks, tobacco, and alcohol-containing mouthwash, which can make dryness worse.
Use fluoride toothpaste and keep up careful brushing, because teeth are more likely to decay when the mouth is dry.
See your dentist or doctor if dryness continues. Do not stop medicines without medical advice.
why: Saliva washes away food, neutralises acids and protects teeth.
Less saliva means more decay, gum problems and mouth discomfort.
Small daily habits can ease dryness.

media.required: Infographic: practical ways to manage dry mouth
media.what: Shows sipping water, sugar-free gum, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and fluoride toothpaste

topics.title: Tooth Sensitivity
bullets: Tooth sensitivity is a short, sharp pain from cold, hot, sweet or touch. It may happen when the softer layer under the enamel is exposed.
Brush gently with a soft brush. Hard brushing can wear away gums and enamel and make sensitivity worse.
Toothpaste made for sensitive teeth may help when used regularly. Ask your dental team which one is suitable.
Limit acidic drinks and foods such as fizzy drinks and citrus, and do not brush straight after acidic foods.
See a dentist if the pain is strong, lasts a long time or wakes you at night, because a cavity or crack can cause similar pain. Do not self-diagnose.
why: Exposed dentine has tiny channels that lead to the tooth’s nerve.
Gentle brushing and the right toothpaste can reduce the discomfort.
Persistent pain needs a dental check, as several problems feel the same.

topics.title: Dental Implants
bullets: Clean around your implant every day, just as you clean your natural teeth. Plaque around an implant can inflame the gums.
Brush twice a day with a soft toothbrush, gently tilting the bristles towards the gum line around the implant.
Clean between the implant and the neighbouring teeth with interdental brushes or implant-friendly floss, in the size your dental team recommends.
Do not use sharp or metal tools on an implant.
Warning signs: red, swollen or bleeding gums around the implant, a bad taste, pus, pain, or a loose implant. See your dentist promptly.
See your dentist for regular check-ups and professional cleaning of the implant. Smoking increases the risk of implant problems.
why: Implants do not decay, but the gums around them can become inflamed.
Early inflammation (peri-implant mucositis) can often be reversed with good cleaning.
If it is not treated, it can damage the bone that holds the implant (peri-implantitis).
warnings: References for this topic: pending clinical review by the dental team.

topics.title: Diabetes
bullets: People with diabetes are more likely to develop gum disease, and gum disease can make blood sugar harder to control.
Good blood sugar control helps protect your gums. Follow your doctor’s advice.
Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between your teeth daily.
Warning signs: red, swollen or bleeding gums, bad breath that does not go away, loose teeth, a dry mouth, or mouth sores that heal slowly.
Tell your dentist that you have diabetes and which medicines you take.
See your dentist regularly. If you smoke, stopping helps your gums.
why: High blood sugar makes it harder for the body to fight infection, including in the gums.
Gum infection can raise blood sugar.
Looking after your mouth is part of managing diabetes.
warnings: References for this topic: pending clinical review by the dental team.

media.what: Shows the two-way link between blood sugar and gum disease, with warning signs

topics.title: Gum Disease (Periodontal Disease)
bullets: **Healthy gums** are pink and firm and do not bleed when you brush. **Gingivitis** means red, swollen gums that bleed easily; it can be reversed with good cleaning.
**Periodontitis** is more serious. Signs include gums pulling away from the teeth, persistent bad breath, pus, and loose or moving teeth.
Brush twice a day with a soft toothbrush, gently tilting the bristles towards the gum line, using light pressure.
Clean between your teeth every day with floss or interdental brushes.
Plaque that hardens becomes calculus (tartar), which only a dental professional can remove by scaling.
Smoking makes gum disease worse. See your dentist for scaling and periodontal treatment, and for regular maintenance visits.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)
why: Gum disease often causes no pain in the early stages.
Plaque control at home and professional cleaning work together.
Untreated periodontitis can lead to tooth loss.

topics.title: Oral Cancer Awareness
bullets: **What is oral cancer?** Oral cancer is a cancer that can start in the lips, tongue, cheeks, gums, floor of the mouth or roof of the mouth. Changes found early are easier to treat.
**Common sites:** the sides and underside of the tongue, the floor of the mouth, the inner cheeks, the gums, the lips and the roof of the mouth.

**Why early detection matters:** oral cancer found early is usually easier to treat and has better outcomes. Many early changes cause no pain, so regular dental check-ups and Mouth Self-Examination (MSE) are important.

**Main risk factors:** smoking, smokeless tobacco, alcohol, chewing betel quid or areca nut, and HPV infection (mainly at the back of the throat). Using tobacco and alcohol together raises the risk further.

**Warning signs:** a mouth ulcer that does not heal, a white patch (leukoplakia), a red patch (erythroplakia), a lump or swelling, ongoing pain, bleeding without a clear cause, difficulty swallowing or moving the tongue, or a lump in the neck.

**When to seek professional help:** see your dentist if any ulcer, patch, lump or other change lasts for more than two weeks. Not every patch or ulcer is cancer, and most mouth ulcers heal by themselves.
**Mouth Self-Examination (MSE):** do it regularly, for example once a month, in front of a mirror, in good light and with clean hands.
**Step 1 – Lips:** look at and feel the inside and outside of your upper and lower lips.
**Step 2 – Inner cheeks:** gently pull out each cheek and check for patches, ulcers or lumps.
**Step 3 – Gums:** look at the gums of your upper and lower teeth, front and back.
**Step 4 – Tongue:** stick out your tongue and check the top, both sides and the underside.
**Step 5 – Floor of the mouth:** lift your tongue and look underneath.
**Step 6 – Roof of the mouth:** tilt your head back, open wide and look at the roof.
**Step 7 – Back of the mouth and throat:** look as far back as is comfortable.
**Step 8 – Neck:** feel both sides of the neck and under the jaw for lumps or swelling.
**Remember:** MSE does not replace a professional dental examination or diagnosis. Do not try to diagnose yourself. See your dentist about any suspicious or persistent change.

Sources: [MOH Malaysia, Program Ikon Gigi (iGG) module](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/garispanduan/Modul%20Ikon%20Gigi%20-%20SET%201.pdf) · [MOH Malaysia Oral Health Programme (oral cancer leaflets)](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/ms/hubungi-kami/sitemap) · [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)

topics.title: Dental Caries
bullets: **What is dental caries?** Dental caries (tooth decay) is damage to a tooth caused by acids that are made when bacteria in plaque break down sugars.

**How it develops:** frequent sugary foods and drinks, poor plaque removal and too little fluoride allow acid attacks to wear away the enamel. Early decay can appear as white spots and may be reversed with fluoride and good care.
**Signs:** white or brown spots, holes in the teeth, sensitivity to sweet, hot or cold, and toothache. Early decay often causes no pain.
**Who is at risk:** anyone who has sugary snacks or drinks often, has a dry mouth, does not clean the teeth well or has exposed tooth roots.
**Prevention:** brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, keep sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes, clean between your teeth and have regular dental check-ups.
**When to seek professional help:** see your dentist if you notice spots, holes or toothache. Early treatment is simpler and saves more of the natural tooth.

**In Malaysia:** the National Oral Health Survey of Pre-School Children 2015 found that 71.3% of preschool children had dental caries, down from 87.1% in 1995 and 76.2% in 2005. Children with caries in their baby teeth are about three times more likely to get caries in their permanent teeth.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)

Sources: [MOH Malaysia, Oral Health Programme: Garis Panduan Perkhidmatan Kesihatan Pergigian Toddler (2022), Appendix 5 Anticipatory Guidance](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/publication/FINAL%20GP%20TODDLER%202022%2010.10.2022.pdf)
why: Dental caries is one of the most common oral diseases worldwide, and it is largely preventable.
Untreated decay can cause pain, infection and tooth loss.
Home care and regular check-ups work together.

media.required: Comparison: healthy tooth vs early decay vs cavity
media.what: Labelled clinical photographs showing a healthy tooth, a white-spot lesion and a cavity

topics.title: Gum Disease
bullets: **What is gum disease?** Gum disease is an infection and inflammation of the tissues that support the teeth. It starts as gingivitis and can progress to periodontitis.
**Gingivitis:** red, swollen gums that bleed easily when brushing. It can be reversed with good oral hygiene.
**Periodontitis:** damage to the gum attachment and the bone around the teeth. It may cause receding gums, loose teeth and bad breath, and it needs professional treatment.
**Risk factors:** plaque build-up, smoking and tobacco use, diabetes, pregnancy and other hormonal changes, some medicines and a family history of gum disease.

**Prevention:** remove plaque every day by brushing and cleaning between your teeth, do not smoke, keep diabetes under control and see your dentist regularly. Practical cleaning steps are in Oral Hygiene Instruction.
**When to seek professional help:** bleeding, swollen or receding gums, loose teeth, or bad breath that does not go away.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)
why: Early gum disease often causes no pain.
Gingivitis can be reversed. Periodontitis can be controlled but the lost support cannot be fully regained.
Gum disease is a major cause of tooth loss in adults.

media.required: Comparison: plaque vs calculus, and healthy gums vs gingivitis
media.what: Labelled clinical photographs side by side

topics.title: Diet and Oral Health
bullets: **Sugar and teeth:** each time you eat or drink sugar, bacteria in plaque make acid that attacks the teeth.
**How often matters:** frequent snacking and sipping sweet drinks cause more acid attacks than sugar eaten as part of a meal.
**Choose:** water as your main drink, and fresh fruit, vegetables, plain milk or unsweetened yoghurt as snacks.
**Limit:** sweetened drinks (including sweetened tea and coffee, soft drinks and packaged juices), sweets, biscuits and sticky foods, especially between meals and at bedtime.
**Acidic drinks** such as fizzy drinks, energy drinks and some fruit juices can wear away enamel. Do not brush straight after having them.
**Babies and young children:** do not add sugar to food or drinks, and do not put a baby to bed with a bottle of milk or a sweet drink.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)
why: How often you have sugar matters as much as how much.
Healthy eating supports healthy teeth and gums.
Water helps wash away food and keeps the mouth moist.

media.required: Infographic: healthy snack and drink choices
media.what: Shows water, fruit, plain milk and unsweetened snacks compared with sugary drinks, sweets and sticky foods

topics.title: Tobacco and Vaping
bullets: **Smoking and tobacco:** cigarettes, cigars and smokeless tobacco increase the risk of gum disease, tooth loss, stained teeth, bad breath and oral cancer.

**Vaping (e-cigarettes):** vaping is not risk-free for the mouth. It can dry the mouth and irritate the gums, and it may contain nicotine, which is addictive. Its long-term effects are still being studied.
**Betel quid and areca nut:** chewing them also raises the risk of oral cancer and gum problems.
**Warning signs:** gums that bleed or recede, white or red patches, ulcers that do not heal and ongoing bad breath. See your dentist if you notice them.
**Quitting helps:** stopping tobacco improves gum health and lowers the risk of oral cancer over time. Ask your clinic about help to quit.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)
why: Tobacco reduces blood flow in the gums and slows healing.
The nicotine in vapes is addictive.
It is never too late to quit.

media.required: Infographic: effects of tobacco, vaping and betel quid on the mouth
media.what: Shows effects on gums, teeth, breath and oral cancer risk, and where to get help to quit

topics.title: Diabetes and Oral Health
bullets: **The two-way link:** people with diabetes are more likely to develop gum disease, and severe gum disease can make blood sugar harder to control.
**Why this happens:** high blood sugar makes it harder for the body to fight infection, and diabetes can reduce saliva.
**Other mouth problems:** dry mouth, mouth sores that heal slowly and fungal infections such as oral thrush.
**Prevention:** keep blood sugar well controlled, follow your doctor’s advice, do not smoke and have regular dental check-ups.

**When to seek professional help:** bleeding or swollen gums, loose teeth, persistent bad breath, dry mouth or mouth sores that heal slowly. Daily cleaning advice is in Oral Hygiene Instruction › Special Oral Care › Diabetes.
why: Gum health and blood sugar affect each other.
Early dental care helps protect your general health.
warnings: References for this topic: pending clinical review by the dental team.

topics.title: Brushing Techniques
notes: Your dentist will advise which technique suits you.

qa.question: Modified Bass Technique
qa.answer:
Animated illustration

Who is it for? Most older children, teenagers and adults.

Cleans along the gum line, where plaque collects.

1
Place your toothbrush gently where your teeth meet your gums.
2
Tilt the bristles slightly towards the gums.
3
Move the brush gently in small, short movements for a few seconds.
4
Sweep the brush towards the chewing surface of the tooth, then move to the next tooth.
Common mistake: Scrubbing hard from side to side.

qa.question: Bass Technique
qa.answer:
Animated illustration

Who is it for? People with gum problems, when your dentist advises.

Cleans just under the gum edge with very small movements.

1
Place the brush where the teeth meet the gums, with the bristles tilted towards the gums.
2
Move the brush in very small, gentle shaking movements without sliding it along the teeth.
3
Move to the next small group of teeth and repeat.
Common mistake: Pressing too hard, which can hurt the gums.

qa.question: Fones Technique
qa.answer:
Animated illustration

Who is it for? Young children, with a parent’s help.

A large circular movement that is easy for small hands.

1
Ask the child to close their teeth gently together.
2
Move the brush in large circles over the outer surfaces of the upper and lower teeth.
3
Open the mouth and brush the inner and chewing surfaces with back-and-forth movements.
Common mistake: Letting a young child brush alone without a parent finishing the job.

qa.question: Stillman’s Technique
qa.answer:
Animated illustration

Who is it for? People with sensitive or receding gums, when your dentist advises.

Gently cleans the gum line and the necks of the teeth.

1
Place the bristles at the gum line, tilted slightly towards the gums, with part of the bristles on the gum and part on the tooth.
2
Move the brush in tiny, gentle shaking movements.
3
Then sweep the brush towards the chewing surface of the tooth.
Common mistake: Pressing firmly on the gums.

qa.question: Charter’s Technique
qa.answer:
Animated illustration

Who is it for? People with braces, gaps between teeth or after gum treatment, when your dentist advises.

Helps clean between the teeth and around appliances.

1
Tilt the bristles towards the chewing surface, away from the gums, so the tips reach into the gaps between the teeth.
2
Move the brush in small, gentle circles or shaking movements.
3
Also clean along the gum line, using the technique your dentist recommends.
Common mistake: Forgetting to brush along the gum line.

topics.title: Dental Floss: Types and Choice
bullets: **Why floss?** A toothbrush cannot reach the sides of teeth where they touch. Cleaning between your teeth once a day removes plaque from these areas.
**Waxed floss** slides easily between tight teeth and is less likely to shred. **Unwaxed floss** is thinner and suits wider spaces, but it can fray.
**Dental tape** is a flat, wider ribbon. It suits wider gaps and sensitive gums.
**Super floss** has a stiff end for threading, a spongy section and regular floss. It is useful for braces, bridges and around implants.

**Floss picks and holders** are easier to hold than loose floss, so they may help children, older adults and people with limited dexterity or braces. A floss threader helps pass floss under bridges and wires.
**Choosing:** the best floss is the one you can use comfortably every day. Ask your dental team which suits your teeth, braces, bridge or implants.

topics.title: Interdental Cleaning
bullets: **Interdental brushes** are small brushes that clean between the teeth. They are often easier than floss when the gap is large enough, and suit people with gum disease or receding gums.
**Sizes:** choose the largest size that slides in gently without force. Different gaps may need different sizes. Ask your dental team to measure them.
**How to use:** angle the brush slightly towards the gum, insert it gently into the gap and move it in and out a few times. Do not force it.
**Braces, bridges and implants:** interdental brushes clean around brackets and wires, under bridges and beside implants. Use floss where the gaps are too tight for a brush.
**Water flossers (oral irrigators)** use a jet of water. They can help people with braces, bridges, implants or limited dexterity as an extra aid, but they do not replace brushing.
**Single-tufted toothbrush:** a small brush with one tuft of bristles, for hard-to-reach places such as behind the last tooth, crowded teeth, braces and implants.

topics.title: Mouthwash
bullets: **Mouthwash is an extra, not a replacement.** It does not replace toothbrushing and cleaning between your teeth.
**Fluoride mouthwash** helps protect against tooth decay. Use it at a different time from brushing, for example after lunch, so that it does not wash away the fluoride from your toothpaste.
**Antiseptic mouthwash** (for example with cetylpyridinium chloride or essential oils) can help reduce plaque and freshen breath as an extra step. Follow the label.

**Chlorhexidine mouthwash** is not for routine daily use. A dentist or doctor prescribes it for a short, defined period, for example after some procedures or for certain gum conditions. Long-term use can stain the teeth and tongue and change taste.
**Alcohol-free mouthwash** is gentler and suits people with a dry or sensitive mouth. Alcohol-containing mouthwash can sting and dry the mouth.

**How to use:** measure the amount on the label, swish for the time stated, then spit it out. Do not swallow it, do not rinse with water straight afterwards, and do not use it straight after brushing. Ask your dentist before giving it to young children.
why: Brushing and cleaning between the teeth remove plaque. Mouthwash only adds to this.
Rinsing straight after brushing can wash away the fluoride left on your teeth.
Chlorhexidine is strong and needs professional guidance.
warnings: Fluoride mouthwash strength and the age from which children may use it: pending verification against current MOH Malaysia guidance.

topics.title: Tongue Cleaning and Other Aids
bullets: **Tongue scrapers and cleaners:** a coating of bacteria and food debris on the tongue is a common cause of bad breath. Clean the tongue once a day, gently, from the back towards the front, with a scraper or a soft toothbrush.
**Denture brushes** have firm bristles shaped for the curves of dentures. Use them with soap or denture cleaner, not ordinary toothpaste, which can scratch.
**Orthodontic toothbrushes** have a V-shaped or grooved bristle pattern to clean around brackets and wires.
**Bridges and retainers:** clean under bridges with super floss, floss threaders or interdental brushes. Clean removable retainers with a soft brush and cool water, as your dentist advises.
If bad breath continues despite good cleaning, see your dentist.
**See also:** [Adaptive Toothbrushes and Aids (Special Needs/OKU)](topic:31)

topics.title: Daily Oral Hygiene Routine
bullets: **Morning:** brush for about two minutes with fluoride toothpaste and clean your tongue. Clean between your teeth if advised.
**Night-time (the most important):** clean between your teeth, then brush for about two minutes with fluoride toothpaste and spit out. Do not eat or drink anything except water afterwards.
**Sequence:** clean between the teeth, brush all surfaces, clean the tongue, spit out the toothpaste without rinsing. Use mouthwash at a different time if advised.

**After meals:** rinse with water. After acidic foods or drinks, wait for some time before brushing. **After vomiting or reflux:** rinse with plain water and wait before brushing, because stomach acid softens the enamel.
**Common mistakes:** brushing too hard or for too short a time, not cleaning between the teeth, rinsing straight after brushing, using a worn toothbrush and skipping night-time cleaning.

topics.title: Adaptive Toothbrushes and Aids (Special Needs/OKU)
bullets: **Every person is different.** Choose aids for the person’s needs with advice from the dental team, and with caregiver help where needed.
**Enlarged handle and foam grip:** a thicker handle, or soft foam tubing slid over the handle, is easier to hold for a weak grip or arthritis.
**Angled handle:** a bent handle helps people who cannot turn the wrist or reach the back teeth. Ask the dental team how to adapt a handle safely.
**Hand strap:** a strap holds the brush in the hand for people who cannot grip, for example after a stroke.
**Powered toothbrush, floss holders and water flossers:** these can help people with limited dexterity. Some people may not tolerate the vibration or noise.
**Cerebral palsy and limited hand coordination:** a stable, comfortable position, a thicker handle and a powered brush may help. A caregiver may need to guide or complete the brushing.
**Parkinson’s disease and stroke:** a thick handle or hand strap helps a weak or shaky grip. Keep sessions short, rest the arm on a table and check for food trapped on the weaker side.
**Intellectual disabilities:** use a calm, fixed routine with simple steps, pictures or a demonstration, and praise. Caregiver help is often needed.
**Physical disabilities and limited mouth opening:** adapt the handle, choose a small-headed or single-tufted brush and ask the dental team about positioning.
**Seek professional help** if there is difficulty swallowing, choking while brushing, mouth pain or sores, or if the mouth cannot be cleaned.

topics.title: Oral Anatomy and Tooth Structure
bullets: **Parts of a tooth:** the crown is the part you can see and the root is anchored in the jawbone. Enamel is the hard outer layer of the crown, dentine lies beneath it, and the pulp in the centre holds nerves and blood vessels.
**Supporting tissues:** the gum surrounds the tooth, and the periodontal ligament and bone hold it in place.
**Your teeth:** adults usually have up to 32 permanent teeth: incisors, canines, premolars and molars. Children have 20 primary (baby) teeth.
**Enamel cannot regrow** once it is lost, but early damage can be strengthened with fluoride.
**Saliva** protects the teeth by washing away food, neutralising acid and supplying minerals.

media.what: Shows enamel, dentine, pulp, root, gum, periodontal ligament and bone in a labelled cross-section

topics.title: Oral Potentially Malignant Disorders (OPMD)
bullets: **What are they?** Oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) are changes in the lining of the mouth, such as white or red patches, that can sometimes turn into cancer. Most do not.
**Examples:** leukoplakia (white patch), erythroplakia (red patch) and oral submucous fibrosis (stiffening of the cheeks, often linked to chewing betel quid or areca nut).
**Warning signs:** white or red patches that cannot be wiped off, a burning feeling with spicy food, a mouth that is hard to open wide, or an ulcer that does not heal.
**Risk factors:** tobacco, betel quid, areca nut and alcohol. Stopping these habits lowers the risk.
**What to do:** do not diagnose yourself. See your dentist about any patch or change that lasts for more than two weeks. Your dentist may monitor it or take a small sample (biopsy).
**See also:** [Oral Cancer Awareness](topic:19)

topics.title: Fluoride Awareness
bullets: **What fluoride does:** fluoride strengthens enamel and helps early decay to repair. It is one of the most effective ways to prevent tooth decay.
**Where it comes from:** fluoride toothpaste, fluoride mouthwash, professional fluoride varnish and, in some places, fluoridated drinking water.
**Professional fluoride:** your dental team may apply fluoride varnish, especially for children and people at higher risk of decay.

**Using it safely:** use the right amount of toothpaste for the age, spit it out, and keep toothpaste out of reach of young children. Swallowing too much while teeth are forming can cause white or brown marks (dental fluorosis).
**See also:** [Choosing the Right Toothpaste](topic:2)
warnings: Fluoride amounts and concentrations by age: pending verification against current MOH Malaysia guidance.

topics.title: Alcohol and Oral Health
bullets: **Alcohol and oral cancer:** drinking alcohol raises the risk of oral cancer, and the risk is higher when it is combined with tobacco.
**Other effects:** alcohol can dry the mouth and irritate the gums, and sweetened alcoholic drinks and mixers can contribute to tooth decay.
**Acid:** some alcoholic drinks are acidic and can wear away tooth enamel.
**Reducing the risk:** limit or avoid alcohol, drink water too, and do not brush straight after acidic drinks.
**When to seek professional help:** ulcers that do not heal, white or red patches, or ongoing mouth pain. Ask your clinic about support to cut down.
Sources: [WHO: Oral health fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/oral-health)

topics.title: Tooth Erosion
bullets: **What is erosion?** Tooth erosion is the loss of enamel caused by acid that does not come from bacteria, such as acidic food and drinks or stomach acid.
**Causes:** fizzy and energy drinks, sports drinks, fruit juices, citrus fruits, and repeated vomiting or acid reflux.
**Signs:** sensitive teeth, teeth that look smooth, shiny or yellow, and worn or rounded edges.
**Prevention:** limit acidic drinks, have them with meals or through a straw, rinse with water afterwards and wait before brushing. Use fluoride toothpaste.
**See your dentist** if you have reflux, repeated vomiting, or teeth that are becoming sensitive or worn.
**See also:** [Daily Oral Hygiene Routine](topic:30)

topics.title: Halitosis (Bad Breath)
bullets: **What is it?** Halitosis is persistent bad breath. It is common and often treatable.

**Causes:** most cases come from bacteria on the tongue and between the teeth and gums. Other causes include gum disease, tooth decay, dry mouth, smoking, dentures that are not cleaned, and some medical conditions.
**What helps:** brush twice a day, clean between the teeth, clean the tongue, clean dentures every day, drink water and avoid smoking.
**Mouthwash** only freshens the breath for a short time and does not treat the cause.
**See your dentist** if bad breath continues despite good cleaning. Your dentist can check for gum disease, decay or other causes and may advise you to see a doctor.
**See also:** [Tongue Cleaning and Other Aids](topic:29)

topics.title: Tooth Eruption and Development
bullets: **Primary teeth** usually start to appear at around six months of age, and most children have a full set of 20 by about three years.
**Permanent teeth** start to come in at about six years of age, beginning with the first molars and the lower front teeth. Primary teeth are lost gradually until about twelve years.
**Wisdom teeth** usually appear between about 17 and 25 years of age. Some do not come through fully and may need review by a dentist.
**Teething** can cause drooling, sore gums and irritability. A clean teething ring may help. Ask your dentist or doctor before using any medicine or gel.
**Timing varies.** If teeth come much earlier or later than expected, ask your dentist.

Sources: [MOH Malaysia, Oral Health Programme: Garis Panduan Perkhidmatan Kesihatan Pergigian Toddler (2022), Appendix 5 Anticipatory Guidance](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/publication/FINAL%20GP%20TODDLER%202022%2010.10.2022.pdf)

topics.title: Dental Trauma and Emergencies
bullets: **If a permanent tooth is knocked out:** pick it up by the crown, not the root, and do not scrub it. If it is dirty, rinse it gently with milk or clean water and try to place it back in its socket. If you cannot, keep it in milk and see a dentist urgently. Do not put a baby tooth back.
**Broken or chipped tooth:** rinse the mouth, keep any fragment in milk and see a dentist soon.
**Toothache:** rinse with warm water, clean gently between the teeth and see a dentist. Do not put aspirin or other medicine on the gum.
**Facial swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing or breathing** need urgent medical attention. Go to the nearest hospital or clinic.
**Prevention:** wear a mouthguard for contact sports, wear a seat belt and avoid biting very hard objects.

media.required: Infographic: what to do if a tooth is knocked out
media.what: Step-by-step: hold by the crown, rinse gently, replace or keep in milk, see a dentist urgently

topics.title: Regular Dental Check-ups
bullets: **Why go regularly?** Many problems, such as early decay, gum disease and oral cancer, cause no pain at first. A check-up finds them early.
**What happens:** your dentist examines your teeth, gums, tongue and the lining of your mouth, may take X-rays when needed, and gives advice on home care.
**How often:** it depends on your risk of dental disease. Ask your dentist how often you should come.
**Bring** a list of your medicines and health conditions, and tell your dentist about any changes in your mouth.
**Children:** take them for a first visit when the first teeth appear, and keep going for regular visits.
**Do not wait for pain:** see your dentist sooner if you have pain, bleeding gums, swelling, a mouth ulcer that does not heal or loose teeth.

topics.title: Dental Myths and Facts
bullets: **Myth:** baby teeth do not matter because they fall out. **Fact:** baby teeth help with eating and speaking and guide adult teeth into place. Decay can cause pain and infection.
**Myth:** brushing harder cleans better. **Fact:** brushing hard can damage the gums and enamel. Gentle, thorough brushing works best.
**Myth:** bleeding gums mean you should stop brushing. **Fact:** bleeding usually means plaque and inflamed gums. Keep cleaning gently and see your dentist if it continues.
**Myth:** only sugar causes cavities. **Fact:** bacteria turn sugars and other fermentable carbohydrates into acid. How often you eat sweet foods matters, and so do plaque removal and fluoride.
**Myth:** mouthwash can replace brushing. **Fact:** it cannot. Mouthwash is only an extra.
**Myth:** vaping is safe for the mouth. **Fact:** vaping is not risk-free. It can dry the mouth and irritate the gums, and it may contain nicotine.
**Myth:** if it does not hurt, my teeth are fine. **Fact:** early decay and gum disease often cause no pain, so regular check-ups are important.

topics.title: Cancer Treatment (Chemotherapy and Radiotherapy)
bullets: **Why it matters:** chemotherapy and radiotherapy to the head and neck can cause mouth sores, dry mouth, infections, taste changes and tooth decay.
**Before treatment:** if possible, see a dentist before cancer treatment starts so that dental problems can be treated first. Make sure your cancer team and your dentist know about each other.
**During treatment:** brush gently with a very soft brush and fluoride toothpaste, rinse with plain water or as advised, and avoid alcohol-containing mouthwash, spicy foods and tobacco.
**Dry mouth and sores:** sip water often, keep the lips moist and ask your team about saliva substitutes or rinses for mouth sores.

**Seek help promptly** for painful mouth sores that stop you eating, white patches, bleeding, swelling, fever or loose teeth. If you have had radiotherapy to the jaws, tell your dentist before any tooth extraction.
warnings: References for this topic: pending clinical review by the dental team.

topics.title: Multiple Medications
bullets: **Why it matters:** many medicines, for example for blood pressure, depression, allergies, pain and bladder problems, reduce saliva and cause dry mouth.
**Effects:** dry mouth raises the risk of tooth decay, gum problems, mouth infections and denture discomfort. Some medicines can also cause gum overgrowth or change taste.
**Oral hygiene:** brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, clean between your teeth, sip water often and avoid sugary drinks. Ask your pharmacist about sugar-free versions of liquid medicines.
**Tell your dentist** about all your medicines, including herbal products, and bring a list to every visit. Do not stop any medicine without asking your doctor.
**See your dentist** if your mouth feels dry or you have sores, gum swelling or a change in taste.
warnings: References for this topic: pending clinical review by the dental team.

ages.title: Infants and Toddlers (0–3 years)

qa.question: How often should I brush?
qa.answer: Brush twice a day once the first tooth appears. Before that, gently wipe the gums with a clean, damp cloth.

qa.question: What type of toothbrush should I use?
qa.answer: A soft, small-headed baby toothbrush. Before teeth appear, use a clean, damp cloth.

qa.question: How much toothpaste should I use?
qa.answer:
A tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste, about the size of a rice grain. An adult applies it.

> Amount and fluoride strength: MOH Malaysia’s 2022 toddler guideline advises brushing at least twice a day with a smear or pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for ages 1 to 4 years. The exact amount for each age and the fluoride strength still need confirmation by the dental team.

qa.question: How should I position my toothbrush?
qa.answer: Hold your baby comfortably with the head supported, and gently lift the lip to see the teeth.

qa.question: What brushing movements should I make?
qa.answer: Use tiny, gentle circles or short back-and-forth movements. The parent or caregiver does the brushing.

qa.question: Which tooth surfaces should I clean?
qa.answer: Clean the outer, inner and chewing surfaces of every tooth, including the back teeth and along the gum line.

qa.question: How should I clean between my teeth?
qa.answer: Once teeth touch each other, ask your dental team how to clean between them.

qa.question: Should I clean my tongue?
qa.answer: Gently wipe the tongue with a clean, damp cloth.

qa.question: What common mistakes should I avoid?
qa.answer: Putting a baby to bed with a bottle of milk or a sweet drink.

qa.question: When should I visit a dentist?
qa.answer: Take your baby for a first dental visit as soon as teeth appear, and see the dentist regularly after that.

qa.question: Primary tooth eruption and teething:
qa.answer:
the first teeth usually appear from around six months. Teething can cause drooling and sore gums, and a clean teething ring may help.

Read more: [Tooth Eruption and Development](topic:38)

qa.question: Bottle-feeding and early childhood caries:
qa.answer:
do not let a baby sleep with a bottle of milk or a sweet drink, and do not add sugar. Move to a cup when your health team advises.

Read more: [Dental Caries](topic:20)

qa.question: Thumb sucking and pacifiers:
qa.answer: sucking is normal in babies. If it continues beyond the toddler years it can affect how the teeth and jaws develop, so ask your dentist for advice. Never dip a pacifier in sugar or honey.

qa.question: First dental visit:
qa.answer:
take your baby when the first teeth appear, and ask the dental team about fluoride and feeding.

Read more: [Regular Dental Check-ups](topic:40)

qa.question: Lift the Lip check:
qa.answer: once a month, gently lift your child’s lip and look at the front teeth. White or brown spots can be the first sign of early childhood caries. See a dentist if you see them.

qa.question: Cleaning a baby’s teeth:
qa.answer: once teeth appear, clean the teeth and gums with a soft toothbrush and plain water after meals and before bedtime. Take your baby for a first dental check before 12 months of age.

notes: **Sources:** [MOH Malaysia, Oral Health Programme: Garis Panduan Perkhidmatan Kesihatan Pergigian Toddler (2022), Appendix 5 Anticipatory Guidance](https://hq.moh.gov.my/ohp/images/pdf/publication/FINAL%20GP%20TODDLER%202022%2010.10.2022.pdf)

ages.title: Preschool Children (4–6 years)

qa.question: How often should I brush?
qa.answer: Brush twice a day, in the morning and before bed, for about two minutes.

qa.question: What type of toothbrush should I use?
qa.answer: A soft toothbrush with a small head and a thick handle that is easy to hold.

qa.question: How much toothpaste should I use?
qa.answer:
A pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, put on the brush by a parent.

> Amount and fluoride strength: MOH Malaysia’s 2022 toddler guideline advises brushing at least twice a day with a smear or pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for ages 1 to 4 years. The exact amount for each age and the fluoride strength still need confirmation by the dental team.

qa.question: How should I position my toothbrush?
qa.answer: Place the brush against the teeth and gums. A parent helps to hold and guide it.

qa.question: What brushing movements should I make?
qa.answer:
Use gentle circles over the outer surfaces (Fones technique), then back-and-forth movements on the inner and chewing surfaces.

Animated illustration

qa.question: Which tooth surfaces should I clean?
qa.answer: Clean the outer, inner and chewing surfaces of every tooth, including the back teeth and along the gum line.

qa.question: How should I clean between my teeth?
qa.answer: A parent flosses where teeth touch, using a floss holder if needed.

qa.question: Should I clean my tongue?
qa.answer: Yes. Gently brush or scrape the tongue to help keep your breath fresh.

qa.question: What common mistakes should I avoid?
qa.answer: Brushing alone without a parent finishing the job, and swallowing toothpaste.

qa.question: When should I visit a dentist?
qa.answer: Visit your dentist regularly for check-ups, and sooner if you have pain, bleeding gums, swelling or any change in your mouth.

qa.question: Primary teeth still matter:
qa.answer: they hold space for the adult teeth. Decay in baby teeth can cause pain and infection.

qa.question: Fluoride varnish:
qa.answer:
your dental team may paint fluoride varnish on the teeth to help prevent decay, especially in children at higher risk.

Read more: [Fluoride Awareness](topic:34)

qa.question: Habits:
qa.answer: long-term thumb sucking or pacifier use can affect the bite. Ask your dentist for help to stop.

qa.question: Healthy eating:
qa.answer:
keep sweet snacks and drinks to mealtimes, and offer water, fruit and vegetables.

Read more: [Diet and Oral Health](topic:22)

qa.question: How often should I brush?
qa.answer: Brush twice a day, in the morning and before bed, for about two minutes.

qa.question: What type of toothbrush should I use?
qa.answer: A soft toothbrush with a small head that can reach the back molars.

qa.question: How much toothpaste should I use?
qa.answer:
A pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste. Spit it out and do not rinse straight away.

> Amount and fluoride strength: MOH Malaysia’s 2022 toddler guideline advises brushing at least twice a day with a smear or pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for ages 1 to 4 years. The exact amount for each age and the fluoride strength still need confirmation by the dental team.

qa.question: How should I position my toothbrush?
qa.answer: Tilt the bristles slightly towards the gums. Take extra care around the new permanent molars at the back.

qa.question: What brushing movements should I make?
qa.answer: Brush every surface in the same order each time so nothing is missed. Use small, gentle movements.

qa.question: Which tooth surfaces should I clean?
qa.answer: Clean the outer, inner and chewing surfaces of every tooth, including the back teeth and along the gum line.

qa.question: How should I clean between my teeth?
qa.answer: Start flossing once teeth touch, with a parent’s help at first.

qa.question: Should I clean my tongue?
qa.answer: Yes. Gently brush or scrape the tongue to help keep your breath fresh.

qa.question: What common mistakes should I avoid?
qa.answer: Rushing, skipping the back molars and brushing too hard.

qa.question: When should I visit a dentist?
qa.answer: Visit your dentist regularly for check-ups, and sooner if you have pain, bleeding gums, swelling or any change in your mouth.

qa.question: Mixed dentition:
qa.answer: baby and permanent teeth are in the mouth together. The first permanent molars appear at about six years, behind the baby teeth, and are often mistaken for baby teeth. Brush them well.

qa.question: Pit and fissure sealants:
qa.answer: a thin protective coating placed on the chewing surfaces of back teeth by a dental professional helps prevent decay in deep grooves.

qa.question: Fluoride varnish and caries prevention:
qa.answer:
ask your dentist whether your child needs fluoride varnish.

qa.question: Sugar reduction:
qa.answer:
choose water and plain milk, and keep sweets for mealtimes.

qa.question: Sports:
qa.answer:
wear a mouthguard for contact sports.

qa.question: Which tooth surfaces should I clean?
qa.answer: Clean the outer, inner and chewing surfaces of every tooth, including the back teeth and along the gum line.

qa.question: How should I clean between my teeth?
qa.answer: Clean between your teeth daily with floss or interdental brushes, including around braces.

qa.question: Should I clean my tongue?
qa.answer: Yes. Gently brush or scrape the tongue to help keep your breath fresh.

qa.question: What common mistakes should I avoid?
qa.answer: Brushing too hard, missing the gum line and frequent sugary drinks.

qa.question: When should I visit a dentist?
qa.answer: Visit your dentist regularly for check-ups, and sooner if you have pain, bleeding gums, swelling or any change in your mouth.

qa.question: Braces:
qa.answer:
brackets and wires trap plaque, so clean around them carefully and use interdental brushes.

Read more: [Braces & Aligners](topic:11)

qa.question: Wisdom teeth:
qa.answer:
they usually appear between about 17 and 25 years of age. If you have pain, swelling or gum covering part of a tooth, see your dentist.

Read more: [Tooth Eruption and Development](topic:38)

qa.question: Sports mouthguards:
qa.answer:
wear a well-fitting mouthguard for contact sports to protect your teeth and lips.

Read more: [Dental Trauma and Emergencies](topic:39)

qa.question: Smoking and vaping:
qa.answer:
both affect the gums and breath, and nicotine is addictive. Ask for help to quit.

Read more: [Tobacco and Vaping](topic:23)

qa.question: Sugary drinks:
qa.answer:
frequent soft drinks, energy drinks and sweetened tea or coffee cause decay and erosion.

Read more: [Diet and Oral Health](topic:22) · [Tooth Erosion](topic:36)

qa.question: Puberty:
qa.answer:
hormonal changes can make the gums more likely to become red and swollen, so clean carefully along the gum line.

Read more: [Gum Disease](topic:21)

qa.question: How often should I brush?
qa.answer: Brush twice a day, in the morning and before bed, for about two minutes.

qa.question: What type of toothbrush should I use?
qa.answer: A soft toothbrush with a small head. A powered toothbrush is also suitable.

qa.question: How much toothpaste should I use?
qa.answer:
A pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste.

> Amount and fluoride strength: MOH Malaysia’s 2022 toddler guideline advises brushing at least twice a day with a smear or pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for ages 1 to 4 years. The exact amount for each age and the fluoride strength still need confirmation by the dental team.

qa.question: How should I position my toothbrush?
qa.answer: Place the brush where your teeth meet your gums, with the bristles tilted slightly towards the gums.

qa.question: What brushing movements should I make?
qa.answer:
Use small, gentle movements with light pressure, then sweep towards the chewing surface (Modified Bass approach).

qa.answer: Pressing too hard, rushing and missing the gum line.

qa.question: When should I visit a dentist?
qa.answer: Visit your dentist regularly for check-ups, and sooner if you have pain, bleeding gums, swelling or any change in your mouth.

qa.question: Gum disease prevention:
qa.answer:
clean between your teeth daily, do not smoke and see your dentist regularly.

Read more: [Gum Disease](topic:21)

qa.question: Dental caries:
qa.answer:
adults can still get decay, including around old fillings and at the gum line. Use fluoride toothpaste.

Read more: [Dental Caries](topic:20)

qa.question: Sensitivity and erosion:
qa.answer:
brush gently and limit acidic drinks.

Read more: [Tooth Sensitivity](topic:15) · [Tooth Erosion](topic:36)

qa.question: Smoking and oral health:
qa.answer:
smoking harms the gums and raises the risk of oral cancer.

Read more: [Tobacco and Vaping](topic:23) · [Oral Cancer Awareness](topic:19)

qa.question: Preventive care:
qa.answer:
regular check-ups and professional cleaning.

Read more: [Regular Dental Check-ups](topic:40)

qa.question: How often should I brush?
qa.answer: Brush twice a day, in the morning and before bed, for about two minutes.

qa.question: What type of toothbrush should I use?
qa.answer: A soft toothbrush. If your grip is weak, choose a thicker or adapted handle or a powered toothbrush.

qa.question: How much toothpaste should I use?
qa.answer:
A pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste.

> Amount and fluoride strength: MOH Malaysia’s 2022 toddler guideline advises brushing at least twice a day with a smear or pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste for ages 1 to 4 years. The exact amount for each age and the fluoride strength still need confirmation by the dental team.

qa.question: How should I position my toothbrush?
qa.answer: Angle the bristles gently towards the gum line. If your hand shakes, rest your elbow on a table.

qa.question: What brushing movements should I make?
qa.answer: Use small, gentle movements with light pressure, especially where the gums have receded and roots are exposed.

qa.question: Which tooth surfaces should I clean?
qa.answer: Clean the outer, inner and chewing surfaces of every tooth, including the back teeth and along the gum line.

qa.question: How should I clean between my teeth?
qa.answer: Use interdental brushes or floss holders daily. Clean dentures as advised if you wear them.

qa.question: Should I clean my tongue?
qa.answer: Yes. Gently brush or scrape the tongue to help keep your breath fresh.

qa.question: What common mistakes should I avoid?
qa.answer: Brushing too hard on exposed roots, and skipping brushing when tired.

qa.question: When should I visit a dentist?
qa.answer: Visit your dentist regularly for check-ups, and sooner if you have pain, bleeding gums, swelling or any change in your mouth.

qa.question: Root caries:
qa.answer:
when the gums recede, the tooth roots are exposed and decay more easily. Use fluoride toothpaste and clean carefully.

Read more: [Dental Caries](topic:20)

qa.question: Dry mouth:
qa.answer:
many medicines reduce saliva. Sip water often and ask your dentist or pharmacist.

Read more: [Dry Mouth](topic:14)

qa.question: Gum recession:
qa.answer:
brush gently with a soft brush so that the gums and roots are not worn away.

Read more: [Gum Disease](topic:21)

qa.question: Tooth loss and dentures:
qa.answer:
keep your natural teeth for as long as possible. Clean dentures every day and take them out at night as advised.

Read more: [Dentures](topic:12)

qa.question: Reduced dexterity and help from carers:
qa.answer:
adapted handles and powered brushes can help, and carers can assist.

Read more: [Adaptive Toothbrushes and Aids (Special Needs/OKU)](topic:31)
